newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court blocks 'Cat in the Hat' parody on O.J.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court blocks 'Cat in the Hat' parody on O.J.

text.p: A federal appeals court Thursday blocked the sale of a book satirising the O.J. Simpson murder trial because it infringed on the copyright of a famous Dr. Seuss children's story.

The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco affirmed a district court injunction prohibiting the publication and distribution of "The Cat NOT in the Hat!" by "Dr. Juice," an allusion to Simpson's nickname.
The book, by Alan Katz and Chris Wrinn, used child-like rhymes and cartoon drawings of O.J. Simpson in a stove-pipe hat to tell the story of Simpson's 1995 double murder trial.

Simpson, the former NFL player, TV personality and actor, was acquitted of murder by a criminal court jury in October 1995 but was found liable in a civil trial for the deaths of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend Ronald Goldman.

Dr. Seuss Enterprises L.P., which owns the copyrights and trademarks of "The Cat in the Hat" and other works by the late Theodor Geisel, filed suit in February 1996 for copyright and trademark infringement.

Geisel, who died in 1991, wrote and illustrated children's books under the pseudonym "Dr. Seuss." First published in 1957, "The Cat in the Hat" featured a whimsical feline in a stove-pipe hat. The cat was one of his best-known characters.
Dove Audio Inc. and Penguin Books USA Inc., which published and sought to distribute the book, argued that the book was a parody and therefore "fair use" of the original work under copyright rules.
Dr. Seuss Enterprises countered that "The Cat NOT in the Hat!" was not a true parody because the book did not deal directly with the contents of Geisel's original story.
Despite the court challenge, Dove and Penguin went forward with the production schedule, printing about 12,000 copies of the book at a cost of $35,500.
In March 1996, a district court judge granted Dr. Seuss Enterprises' request for a preliminary injunction, blocking the distribution and sale of the books. Dove and Penguin appealed that decision.
In its ruling Thursday the appeals court upheld the district court's preliminary injunction, prohibiting the publication and distribution of the infringing work.
"These stanzas and the illustrations simply retell the Simpson tale," the court wrote.
Simpson is depicted 13 times in the cat's distinctively scrunched and somewhat shabby red and white stove-pipe hat, but the court said "there is no effort to create a transformative work."
An attorney for Dr. Seuss Enterprises said the ruling was a victory for Geisel's widow and her late husband's work.
"It was completely unpalatable to her that anyone would use his work in that fashion," said attorney Cathy Bencivengo.
She said Dr. Seuss Enterprises now hopes to make the injunction permanent.
An attorney for Dove and Penguin said he may appeal.
